title: Education Curious Pedagogy (Jennifer & George) The Unknown Can Be a Scary Space
author: Curious Pedagogy
summary: Written from a college instructor's perspective, this piece uses the Scaredy Squirrel children's book as an extended metaphor to explore why students fear venturing into the unknown and how instructors can help them develop strategies to do so. The authors trace their own journeys from risk-averse students to scholars and use this personal context to make the case for epistemic humility -- positioning oneself at the borders of uncertainty -- as a teachable, practicable skill. The piece examines the tension students feel between the value of learning by failing and the real pressures of a grading system, and offers several pedagogical strategies: scaffolding, transparent learning goals, timely feedback, and metacognitive reflection. The authors address AI as a double-edged tool -- a potential risk-avoidance shortcut for transactional students, but a legitimate support for genuine scholarly exploration when used critically. The article ultimately argues that curiosity and willingness to explore the unknown are not innate traits but learnable stances that instructors must deliberately cultivate.
points: * Epistemic humility -- positioning oneself at the borders of uncertainty -- is not a permanent trait of naturally curious students but a skill that instructors must deliberately teach and give students structured opportunities to practice. * The Dunning-Kruger insight applies directly to student scholarly identity: students who know a little may believe they know a lot, and learning what you don't know is both the hardest and most essential metacognitive move in becoming a knowledge-creator. * Students face a real tension between the educational value of productive failure and the high-stakes reality of grades and admissions -- and instructors who ignore this tension will fail to help students navigate it. * Building community and trust in a course is not incidental to curiosity development: students will only take the risk of asking an unanswerable question if they believe the instructor will not punish them for an honest, evidence-grounded attempt. * AI presents a new risk: the default for transactional students is to use it to blow through the checklist -- eliminating the productive struggle that defines genuine inquiry. For a student becoming a scholar, AI can support exploration, but only if used critically.
quotes: I very much remember being terrified to reach out of my comfort zone as a student. Of course, I would have nodded agreeably as I read Professor Cusack's letter inviting me to think of myself as a scholar, but it would have made me very nervous.
Our students join us at college somewhere on the road between safe, transactional approaches to their work and the curiosity and risk required to become knowledge creators.

Students feel (and the literature on Academic Risk Taking notes) the tension between a 'learning by failing' model and the real pressures of a system where grades matter, if not in an individual course, then to graduate school admissions committees or for entry level employment.
In my biology courses I remind students frequently that we are literally looking for new, unexpected, and 'weird' things rather than trying to recreate scientific findings from the lab cookbook.
Knowing what you don't know is key to learning.
I spend a lot of time building trust and community so students know that I will not punish them for asking a good question and having the universe answer back with a resounding 'Nope.'

AI has the potential to support students in their exploration in ways that are customized to their particular situation and the bounds of their current knowledge. After all, struggle can be unproductive.
